<!-- The manual of coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js: what it does stage by stage and the reason for each rule
     in force. Rewritten 2026-10-08 for the redesign built from process-engineering/batch-redesign.md, which holds
     the evidence and the cost of each new choice; the manual before it, with the history of every rule since
     2026-09-19, is in git at cd2393a08. -->

# The batch workflow script, stage by stage

The script runs one batch of the compile-ladder climb. Everything a batch changes lies between its `MANIFEST` and `END MANIFEST` lines, which the batch's generator writes (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-<N>/manifest/`). The rest of the script is the same for every batch. The practice it builds, and why, is `process-engineering/batch-redesign.md`.

In one paragraph: each rung's worker does its rung test first in its own seeded worktree. Its skeptic checks it and fixes what it finds, test first. A judge rules only on a fix the skeptic marks contested, on a rung it cannot fix, or on a worker's stop, and one repair round runs only on the judge's word. The gather lands the approved rungs on `main`. The merged-diff review and the gate run side by side. The commit stage lands the gate's tables, runs the quick microGPT walk check and pushes. The batch writes no skill text: the skill writer writes the skill from the batch's revival-change material after the landing, and a cold read follows ("After the landing: the coordinator's routing", step 4). Every agent runs on Opus but a judge's second ruling on the same rung or tree, which runs on Fable (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The roles").

## The manifest and the scatter

Per rung, the manifest gives:

- `id`, `slug`, `path` (its worktree), `branch` (`wip/<slug>`) and `title`;
- `blurb`, one line for the batch table every agent reads;
- `section`, the rung's section of the batch record word for word, which every role on the rung reads;
- `pointsToReport`, the kinds of change the curator reviews after the landing;
- `briefing`, the `facts-extract.sh` keys the worker reads first, with `reasons`, one line per key, rendered at the end of the worker's brief;
- `checks`, the sub-list of the briefing that the skeptic, a judge and a repair round read;
- `expectedMinutes`, which only orders the scatter;
- `writesState`, `testIsStage`, `gateJoins` (a gate step the rung brings, such as `testSpecData`), `expectedMoves` (ladder moves declared), and the optional `landsOnlyWith`, `expectedCheckerCount` and `expectedCheckerCrash`.

The script refuses at load a rung without its required fields, a key holding a double quote, backtick, dollar sign, backslash or newline (each is rendered in double quotes), a `checks` key not in the briefing, and `reasons` that are not one line per key.

The scatter starts the longest expected worker first. Two agents run at once on this box and a freed slot goes to the next queued agent (the `cloud-container` skill's `references/machine.md`, "The machine"), so the longest-first order saves up to the shortest worker's time at the end. The gather keeps the manifest's order for its own reading and applies the rungs in its own order (below).

`landsOnlyWith` names the rungs a rung lands only with. After the scatter, a rung any of whose named rungs is not approved is withheld, repeated until nothing moves; it reaches the gather as not landed, and its expected moves and checker declarations stop counting at the gate. Batch 6's T, the number chapters, landed only with F, the flat library they describe. The gather applies such a rung after the rungs it names ("Gather", "The order").

## What a batch commits

A batch commits on a `wip/` branch what it commits on `main`, and nothing else. That is the Fortress change (source, library, specification text, tests) and its reports: `REPORT.md`, `SKEPTIC.md`, `JUDGE.md`, a decision record where the section asks for one, and the batch's `RECORD.md`. It also commits the ledger rows, the FACTS, PLAN and handover lines, each rung's revival-change material in the batch's `RECORD.md`, and a script that is reusable. It commits nothing under `.claude/`: only the skill writer edits the skills (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`). No captured output, log, probe program or copy of a script is committed. An agent's scratch lives under its worktree's `tmp/`, which git ignores and which goes with the worktree, never in the session's scratchpad, which every agent of a run shares: every brief's head says so, since in climb batch 24 eight of the 18 agents wrote files there, and two skeptics one file name (`reviews/batch-24-review.md`, finding 8). Whether a worker wrote its test first and saw it fail is read in its transcript, which the backup keeps (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "While it runs"; `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md`, "What to commit").

## Preparing a batch record

An Opus planning worker drafts `CLIMB-BATCH-<n>.md`. A Fable reviewer edits it in place with one reason per change. The coordinator reads the diff and brings the record's questions to the curator one per message. The batch launches on the answers or on the standing go (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The go").

The planner builds each rung's briefing as in-context learning: the agents were not trained on Fortress, and the language was never finished (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The workflow"). A briefing holds what the rung's section cites: the decisions and earlier rulings it rests on, its ledger rows, the specification's sections whole by their headings, the notes on the subject by section, and the library code that is the precedent. Process positions and harness facts stay out, because the brief's role text and the skill carry them. In batch 10 the workers named none of the 87 POSITIONS and FACTS keys before their fix edits (`process-engineering/context-study.md`, section 5). Each key goes through `facts-extract.sh --check` on the base, every key matching exactly one place. Each carries one line on why it is there. The planner marks the `checks` sub-list: the decisions and rows the checks need, and the sections and precedent code they compare against.

A rung that changes what an implementation does is briefed with the Appendix I Effects and the specification's notes that its change makes false, found by a grep while the record is prepared. Batch 9's record gave rung K none, and Appendix I's `comprises` Effect was that batch's one blocking finding (`reviews/batch-9-review.md`, finding 3).

A record asks a rung for no corpus-wide output comparison, no ladder before-run, no microGPT check and no specification build log (P-103, "The suite's verdict is the check."; the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "What a brief holds"). Whole suites are the skill's rule (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). A count of the programs a change reaches, when a decision needs one, is the planner's probe, taken before the record is written. A named one-time count of changed outputs is asked only where a decision of the curator's names it for that rung. The coordinator starts its base pass before the launch (`tools/count-run/count-run.sh`).

A ledger note that the record briefs fits its row: the planner reads the row with `ledger.py show N` against the tool's limits (notes 700 characters, the row 1,200) and, where the note does not fit, briefs the row's whole new line. Climb batch 26's record briefed rung S a note to row 440, whose notes held 676 of 700 characters (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 6).

The record's section on how it is run gives the manifest's fields rung by rung, the intro every agent reads, and the launch steps. It holds no copy of the block: the batch's generator writes the block from the record.

## Before the launch

The coordinator, in this order:

1. The script, this manual and the batch's manifest generator on `main`. The base is `main`'s head after them, by its full hash, passed as `args.base`.
2. The batch's one base build, a worktree at the base outside the main tree, built once and then left alone. Every rung worktree is seeded from it, and the old code runs from it (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The workflow"). About 200 s, as the skill's `worktrees.md`, "Finding or building a base build", gives it:

        git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add --detach /home/user/fortress-base<N> <base>
        cd /home/user/fortress-base<N>      # then set up the call as the skill's build-and-caches.md says
        ant compileAll                      # BUILD SUCCESSFUL
        # the library order (build-and-caches.md, "The library order"), then one walk run, which warms walk's caches:
        bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
        git status --porcelain              # empty: the seed refuses a base build that is not clean

   Its path goes to the launch as `args.baseBuild`. The script refuses to start without it (scenario B1).
3. One trial seed proves the base build, about 3 s: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh /home/user/fortress-base<N> /home/user/fortress-seedcheck - <base>`, then `git -C /home/user/fortress worktree remove /home/user/fortress-seedcheck`. One `old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base<N> /home/user/fortress-seedcheck-caches ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss`, run from the main tree, proves the old code runs; its folder is removed after.
4. The briefings checked on the base (`python3 explorations/compile-ladder/plan-<N>/manifest/lists<N>.py`). The block generated (`gen<N>.py`), checked in a scratch copy and spliced (`check<N>.js`, then `check<N>.js --write`). Then `node explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js` on the spliced script, which also checks that every skill section the script cites by name is a heading of the skill. Then the commit.
5. `df -h /` against one seeded worktree per rung (about 206 MB each) and the base build. `git status --porcelain` empty in the main tree, and no other agent writing there or pushing `main` while the run gathers and commits. The session's permission rules let the commit stage run `tools/mg-run.sh`.
6. Check-ins armed for the run's length, 45 minutes apart (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "Watching a run").

The launch: `Workflow({scriptPath: 'explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js', args: {base: '<full hash>', baseBuild: '/home/user/fortress-base<N>'}})`. The args are kept byte for byte, since a resume needs them. The base build stays until the coordinator removes it after the landing.

## The brief, which replaced the shared prefix

Until batch 10 every brief opened with one shared prefix of 47K characters, on the premise that the agents shared its cache. They did not: across agents the prompt cache serves the system prompt and tools, and the first message only when the whole prompt is identical (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "The Workflow tool").

Every brief now opens with a head of about 4K characters:

- the batch's intro;
- the pointer to the `fortress-repo` skill for how to work: set up a call, build, run the old code beside the new, write and run tests, wait, stop processes, commit and report; and the part on how revived Fortress differs, read whole before work, which its `SKILL.md` says every task needs, described and not named, since the scenario checker refuses a brief that names a path under `.claude/skills/` ("No skill text"; `tools/workflow-scenarios.js`). In climb batch 25, with the head naming no part, 9 of the 20 agents read it, against 20 reads in 18 agents at climb batch 24 (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 8);
- the batch table, one line per rung;
- the base build and how the old code runs from it;
- the points to report;
- how to cite: the tree at `file:line`, a FACTS or POSITIONS entry by its bold title, a result by two to five quoted lines and the command;
- where the agent's scratch goes: under the `tmp/` of the worktree its role works in, in the folder its role names or one named for its role, never in the session's scratchpad ("What a batch commits");
- what to do after a compaction: re-read the brief, the first message of the agent's own transcript, and the files it wrote; the coordinator's boot is not the agent's;
- two rules beside the skill: each part of the skill opened in a call of its own, since a call's output past 30,000 characters is saved to a file under a 2K preview and takes another call to read (17 results of climb batch 26, most of them several parts in one `cat`); and each `wait_for` call sent alone in its message, since calls sent together hold the turn until the last returns: climb batch 26's gate sent two, went 481 s without a request, past an agent's five-minute prompt cache, and wrote 94K again (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding s 2 and 4).

The role's own part follows. It says what the role does in this batch and where, and points to the skill's parts by name for the how. Where brief and skill differ, the brief says so and holds.

A long step a brief starts in the background (the rung's distance after, the gate's distance stage, the commit stage's microGPT walk check, the gather's build, harness runs, demos and specification build on the merged tree) is written in the literal form of the skill's `session.md`, "Long commands": `nohup bash -c '( COMMAND ) > LOG 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> LOG' >/dev/null 2>&1 &`, waited for with `wait_for`, called again in a call of its own, sent alone in its message, until it prints `EXIT=`. In climb batch 25 the gather, whose brief named no way to wait, waited twice for 600 s in the foreground on the demos, and each next call wrote its whole context again, 708K, 11.7 % of the run's writes (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 1). No brief names `run_bg`: the session's automatic permission check refused it at all nine of its uses in climb batch 11, in eight agents, since it cannot read the command the function passes to `bash -c`, and the literal form passed (`reviews/batch-11-review.md`, section 3).

The worker reads its rung's whole briefing as its second step, each part in a call of its own: climb batch 26's rung S printed parts 2 and 3 in one call, 32.9K, which the tool saved to a file, and read them only by `grep` (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 4). The skeptic, a judge and a repair round read the `checks` sub-list. A repair on the merged tree reads the `checks` of the rungs its ruling names, and none where it names none.

A rung worker makes its own worktree: nobody makes one at the launch. The brief gives the one command, `seed-worktree.sh <base build> <worktree> <branch> <base>`. It reuses a worktree that exists and a branch already pushed, otherwise cuts the branch from the base, and seeds the build and caches in about 3 s. If it exits 2, the worker builds as `worktrees.md` says and reports it.

## Rung worker

The order of work: seed the worktree; read the briefing; the test first (`tests-writing.md`, "The order"); where the fix belongs, with every way listed; the edit and the build it needs; whole suites only as `tests-running.md` says; the count and distance stages where the section asks and the edit can move them; the three homes of every defect (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded"); competing declarations; the change's own ladder subset (`gate.md`, "The ladder regression"); the specification's text in the S1 form, with every sentence the change makes false listed.

- The test and the fix may share a commit; the order is read in the transcript (P-102, "Test first, the test kept.").
- A new ledger row goes in `record.md` in `ledger.py`'s row template, numbered `NEW-<rung>-<n>` and cited so in tests and reports. The worker never runs `ledger.py add`, `note`, `rewrite` or `close`: `add` numbers a row max + 1, so two branches that each add a row would collide (`gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, D7). The gather numbers them. A note it gives only where the row with it stays within `ledger.py`'s limits (notes 700 characters, the row 1,200), else the row's whole new line, and it lints each row line it gives with `ledger.py check --rows`, which writes nothing: in climb batch 26 six row writes were refused for length at the gather (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 6).
- `record.md` carries, as complete findings, the FACTS entry the rung earns, its ledger notes, the whole new line of each row whose claim its change alters, its new rows, the handover line, and a "Revival change" section, or "Revival change: none" with the reason. The section is material for the skill writer, not skill text, in two labelled parts: "The change", as evidence (the team's source and what it says or does, with `file:line`; what the tree now does, with its test; the reason, as a passage, a checker refusal or a measured failure), and "Provenance" (the question or item, the answer or default it follows, the batch). The worker is told: "Name no question, item, batch, rung or record file in the change, and give no decision's status there; provenance goes in its own part." (the `coordinator` skill's `references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"; `reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "Proposed fix to the mechanism", item 2.)
- `REPORT.md` opens with five provenance lines: problem, spec, precedent, deviation, historical. The `historical:` line names every file of the 2012 tree the rung edits, for the commit message (the protocol's hard rule on the gate).
- The worker does not edit FACTS, the ledger, PLAN, POSITIONS, INDEX, the handover, the tools or `.claude/`: the gather folds `record.md` into them, since every rung would conflict there.
- It commits and pushes its own files on its branch as it goes, so a dead container loses nothing.
- A resume after a kill runs it again from its start with the same brief, which no retry's head reaches (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "Interrupts and process stops"). So step 1 of the brief says that the commits past the base, or in a resume or repair round those after the one that carries the judge's ruling, and the uncommitted edits are its earlier launch's; that the head it reached is the newest of those commits; and where that launch's transcript is, with any extract of it under the worktree's `tmp/`. In climb batch 23 both resumed workers found their predecessors' transcripts on their own and wrote their extracts in the session's scratchpad, and rung W ran its tests on the base's code again (`reviews/batch-23-review.md`, findings 2 and 4).
- It writes `REPORT.md`, `record.md` and a decision record through a Bash heredoc or a script, not the `Write` tool: in climb batch 24 the harness refused the `Write` of `REPORT.md` to four of the seven workers, 'Subagents should return findings as text, not write report files.', and none of the three that wrote it through a heredoc (`reviews/batch-24-review.md`, finding 5).
- Its result carries `reportText` and `recordText` word for word, since the harness often refuses a worker's write of those files; `decisions`, each with the ways not taken, which its skeptic weighs its fixes against; `pointsReached`; and `forCurator`, its questions for the curator.
- A point to report is listed with its evidence, and the rung lands. Only a step that cannot be undone or acts against a decision on record is not taken: the worker stops and says which (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs").

A result of the base's code that the section or briefing gives, a planner's probe among them, is the worker's before, as the landed tables are a stage's: the worker runs that probe on its code only. In climb batch 25 rung C ran the planner's code-generator probe on the base again for a comparison in one session, which a count of refusals does not need (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 6). Its `REPORT.md` names the commit each stage ran on, and says so where a change of code followed the stage's start: climb batch 26's rung T ran its count one code commit before its last and called the table its final tree's (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 8).

A rung that edits only prose has no test and no failure to see. Its text is checked against the tree and the decisions on record. A `testIsStage` rung's test is the checker count or distance stage, run once after its edit and rebuild, its before the last landed gate's table. A rung that changes the compiled checker also times the count stage on the base build before its edit and on its tree once the change is correct, in one session, then makes the second pass that the skill's `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", asks for, which makes the checker faster and keeps its results the same; the brief says that section holds where the brief differs (P-148, "The checker's speed comes right after its correctness.").

## Skeptic

The skeptic checks the rung and fixes what it finds, so that the rung lands right with no repair round after it (`process-engineering/batch-redesign.md`, "The skeptic that fixes what it finds").

First it writes the worker's `REPORT.md` and `record.md` onto the branch from the run's journal, where the branch lacks them (`tools/journal-text.py`), commits them alone, and reads them there. Its brief carries the worker's structured result without those texts. It reads the `checks` slice and lists the worker's transcript with two `jq` programs: one lists a transcript's edits, commits, builds and harness runs with their times and call ids, the other prints one call.

Its 11 checks:

1. the count and distance tables, each stage's start read against the worker's last change of code, or the paths that show neither stage could move;
2. test first, read in the transcript by time and call id;
3. the diff against the section, the specification and the decisions;
4. where the fix belongs, and the library's way;
5. the test and its citations;
6. its own programs on the old and new code, at one and four threads where the diff touches mutable state;
7. the three homes;
8. the ledger and the sibling sites;
9. the report, its provenance lines, the whole-suite run, the points to report, and `record.md` true as written;
10. competing declarations;
11. the failure-mode question.

It builds nothing to check. It runs its own programs with the rung's build and the old code from the base build (`worktrees.md`, "Running the old code"), and reads the worker's suite runs and stages in the transcript. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, it also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's head in one session, and checks the two times and that its table and output equal those of the worker's run before the second pass (the skill's `compiler.md`, "The checker's time").

What it does with a finding:

- **A correction** it makes and commits. An assertion or a test it adds is seen failing on the base's code through the old code tool and passing on the head (`worktrees.md`, "Running the old code"): the fix is already in the tree, so the base is where it fails. A test of a defect it finds, a correction's or a fix's, goes in the test folder for its kind that the skill's `tests-writing.md`, "Where a test goes, and how it passes", gives, `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a compiled one, whatever the section's list of files says, and where that list lacks the folder its path is listed for the curator, as a path outside the section is (below). In climb batch 24 skeptic W left rows 865 and 866 with reproducer `none`, since its section's files did not give it `compiler_tests/` (`reviews/batch-24-review.md`, finding 3).
- **A defect of the change** it fixes test first: a gated test or assertion seen failing on the worker's head, the fix, one build, the test seen passing, and the whole suite the fix reaches once after its last fix. Each fix is a commit titled "Skeptic's fix:", pushed. No count or distance stage runs after a fix: the gate's tables on the merged tree are the record.
- **A settled fix** cites the sentence of the section, the specification or a decision on record that settles it.
- **A contested fix** is still made, in its own commit, and listed with the worker's argument and the skeptic's. A fix is contested when the worker's report argues for the behaviour it changes, when nothing on record settles it, or when it touches a path outside the rung's section that no cited sentence settles. A settled fix that reaches a point to report or a path outside the section is not contested for that: it lands, and the point or the path is listed for the curator (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The roles").
- **A refusal** comes only when the rung cannot be fixed here: the approach is wrong; the fix needs a path no rung may touch, or a decision of the curator; or it is larger than a repair round.

A resume after a kill runs it again from its start, as it runs the worker, so its brief, like the worker's, says that the commits after the worker's last one that carry the worker's texts, a `Skeptic's fix:` or `SKEPTIC.md`, and its files under `tmp/<slug>/skeptic/`, are its earlier launch's, to take over and not redo, and where that launch's transcript is. In climb batch 25 the restart killed skeptic P 8 minutes in, and its second launch wrote its programs again from the start: the first launch's 229K was lost (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 2).

It writes `SKEPTIC.md`, through a heredoc or a script as the worker does, and commits it alone, last. Its verdict is `approved`, `contested` or `refused`. It returns `headJudged` (the worker's head), `headAfter`, its fixes and contested fixes, and `leftForGather`. Its `skepticText` is the word `committed` once `SKEPTIC.md` is committed, and the text only where the harness refused the write.

There is no second skeptic (`batch-redesign.md`, "No second skeptic"). The merged-diff review reads every fix and repair commit in its maker's transcript.

## Judge and repair round

# Running and reviewing a batch

The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.

**batch record**
: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.

**base**
: Commit that the batch starts from.

**gather**
: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.

**merged-diff review**
: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.

**repair round**
: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.

**commit stage**
: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.

**reserved point**
: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.

**revival page**
: Page that tells where the revival stands: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/revival-story.md` and its rendered `revival-story.html`, published at the URL that `explorations/coordinator/tools/revival-page/update.py` names, with a GitHub Pages copy under `docs/revival-story/`.

**checker count**
: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library. The gate's distance stage counts them (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`), and FACTS holds the current value.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

Until the switch-over lands, the gate of every batch reports the checker count and the distance. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

## Reserved points and repairs

- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.

## While it runs

- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
- From the launch until the run ends, by landing, by stopping or by holding its push for the curator, edit no tracked file in the main tree, the boot note included. The gather needs `git status --porcelain` there to print nothing. Keep `origin/main` at or behind the main tree's head, or git refuses the commit stage's push. So push `main` from no other tree. From the main tree, push nothing that the batch committed: the commit stage pushes it.
- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.
- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.

## The landing

The landing check is `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, run by the gather and by the merged-diff review on the batch's base. It reports a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test removed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status. A finding the base already had counts too. The gather clears each finding before its commit, through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or by a reworded entry. The merged-diff review clears any that is left in its corrections commit. So a batch lands only when the check prints nothing.

If the batch's push is held for the curator, take steps 1 to 3 at once on the local commits. Only these wait: the push, the parts of step 3's routing check that need the pushed hashes, and step 4, since the record-landing workflow pushes `main` itself. After the curator's go, push the batch yourself, by `fortress-repo`'s committing part. The review's commit of step 3 goes with that push. Then run step 4.

1. Sweep the batch agents' to-dos from the session's shared task list: `explorations/coordinator/tools/sweep-tasks.py --delete`. If another workflow still runs, add `--running`, which removes only the completed tasks. The agents write these to-dos themselves, and the harness shows the whole list to every agent.
2. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
3. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing"). Have the review's section on cost count the tokens written in three spans, each on its own. Give the reviewer each span as two times, read from the commits and the workflow journals:

   - the landing work of the batch before: from its commit stage's last commit to the end of its record-landing workflow;
   - the preparation: from then to the launch of the batch under review;
   - the run: from that launch to its commit stage's last commit, which stands also while the push is held.

   Have the reviewer count a span as `spend.py` from its start less `spend.py` from its end, over the same folders. A transcript then counts in the span where it last changed.
4. After the post-batch review is committed, run the record-landing workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`). It brings FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, PLAN and the review queue in line with the landing. Its Land stage, the step that lands its commits on `main`, also pushes them. Then it runs the orientation workflow in update mode itself, on the entries that the landing added or changed. The orientation workflow writes new text for each section of `fortress-repo`'s `revival-changes.md` that these entries touch. Next, the workflow has the skill writer install the sections that the orientation judge accepts. The writer also brings in line the sentences of `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` and other parts that the landing's changes to FACTS and POSITIONS made false, and no others. A new rule, or a change of a rule's meaning, is not made in the workflow: the writer lists it for you in its reports, `writer-1.md` and `writer-2.md` in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/skills/`. After the workflow ends, judge each such rule on its merits: what it protects against what it costs, its ground, and whether the skill already covers it. Then take it or drop it. Give the rules that you take to your own skill writer. They land after their cold read and the writer's fixes (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"). Name the rules that you dropped, with their reasons, in one line of the message that sends the curator the one line for the page of `fortress-repo` changes (below). The workflow runs a cold read of the writer's changes, and the writer fixes its flags. Then it has a worker update the page of `fortress-repo` changes (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7), and pushes the writer's commits, as its Land stage pushes the record's. Last, if every push went through, it updates the revival page with `update.py`, commits and pushes the files that the script names, and republishes the page. No step of yours comes between. Its result gives one line: the commits and the link of the page of `fortress-repo` changes (the README, "The skill update"), then the revival page's commit and version (the README, "The revival page"). If the landing made no sentence of the skill false and the orientation judge did not run, no writer starts, and the line names only the revival page. While the workflow runs, start no skill-writer task of your own on `fortress-repo`.

   Then read the workflow's commits on `main`, as the README's "Landing its result" says. If the result's `stopped` is set, take the step that the README gives for it there, or, for the revival page, in "The revival page": a stopped push leaves the commits on the local `main`, for you to push or take off. If a page's agent could not publish, the line names that page's files and URL: publish them yourself by that URL. File the orientation update's held sections, in its `queue.md`, in the review queue. Ask whether you would have done anything differently. Tell the curator of its POSITIONS changes as `SKILL.md`, "Quiet times", says. Send the curator the one line for the page of `fortress-repo` changes (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions") when "Quiet times" allows: while the curator is away, hold it with the reports of skill changes. Once the reviews show the workflow sound, stop this review, and rely on what the workflow does.

232	
233	### The words this record uses
234	
235	- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** checks a program's types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**. Until the **switch-over**, the compiled path uses its own small library, the **prelude**. After it, the compiled path uses the interpreter's library, the **one library**.
236	- A **native binding** is a library declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. Its string names a **glue class**, which only walk can call, or a **helper**, a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, which both paths call (P-58). A **carrier** is the Java type in which walk passes a declared type to a helper. A **bare binding** is a native binding at types that a carrier takes.
237	- A **pair** is a public declaration over a wide type that converts its argument in Fortress and calls a bare binding at a narrow type (P-162).
238	- **The count** and **the distance** are the checker's errors on the one library: the count on its main component, the distance on its fourteen core components. Both are 0 (F-53).
239	- A **rung** is one change, built by one worker and checked by a second agent, the skeptic. A **batch** is a few rungs landed together after the **gate**. The **gather** composes the rungs on `main`. A **guard** is a test that passes before the change and after it.
240	- **Appendix I** is the specification's appendix of changes. A revised passage carries a **callout** that names its entry there.
241	- **microGPT** is the model program, by which the revival is measured: two Fortress programs, each with a quick check beside it. A **model line** is a source line of either; no rung of this batch changes one.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:74
- P-167 **The three natives over `Any`: `ilkName` and `SEQV` name the compiled path's helpers, which walk's loader answers with its own operations, and `Object`'s `asString` is written in Fortress as `self.ilkName`.** `ilkName` and `SEQV` keep P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")`, naming `stringOps.typeName` and `equality.sEquiv`. The compiled path runs each helper as it does today, and the helper's answer is the operation's definition. Walk's loader (`interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java`, where it reads a `builtinPrimitive` string) holds a table of the two names and answers each with walk's own operation, as a virtual machine runs its own code for an intrinsic; no implementation is shared, and one test runs on both paths to hold the two together. For these two names P-58's walk half, that walk loads the named helper, bends. `Object`'s `asString` becomes `self.ilkName`, P-91's rule as text, which removes one native and the compiled stack overflow of row 321. The ilk is the trait's name on both paths, such as `ZZ32` and never walk's `Int`, so walk's native objects stop being types that a program sees or prints; the rung works out the way. What `SEQV` answers is P-168. Why: the compiled path's answer is the definition and walk is brought in line, the curator's "do it the way the compiler path does it"; the three are the runtime's own operations, not calls into Java helpers. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 6, options (c) and (e1).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:98
- P-168 **What `SEQV` means, on both paths: the specification's rule, with no special case for any type.** Values of different types are never strictly equivalent; two value objects of one type are when their fields are, tuples element by element and floats by their bit patterns; two reference objects are only when they are one object (`Specification/basic/objects.tex`, "Object Equivalence" and "Value Objects"). Both paths read the `value` modifier. Each path changes its own code: walk drops its equivalence across types (row 909) and its answer `true` for value objects whose body declares no field (row 113); the compiled helper `equality.sEquiv` gains the rule for value objects, tuples and floats (rows 906 to 908). `ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects (P-166). Strings are reference objects: the library declares `FlatString`, `CatString` and `SubString` without `value`, so two such strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and text equality is the strings' own `=`. This overrules the team's code on both paths, walk's `seqv` and the prelude's `opr ===(a:String, b:String) = a=b`, where the specification is silent on strings. The rung's first test is a program with a `value object CC64`, run on both paths beside the review's 14 cases. Why: the specification's rule read as written, over the team's unfinished code of 2008 and 2010, which its authors called preliminary and incomplete; P-167 makes this one comparison that both paths answer. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4; `reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md`, sections 3 and 7.

POSITIONS.md:97
- P-166 **`ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects, and the specification's list of reference objects stops naming arbitrary-precision numbers.** The library declares `value object BigNum extends ZZ` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:565`, `.fsi:223`), so every `ZZ` value is a value object, and `QQ`'s object `Ratio` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:664`), a plain object today, becomes a `value object` too (row 911, the two declarations that disagree). By the specification's rule two value objects of one type are strictly equivalent when their fields are, so two `ZZ` values built apart are `SEQV` when their integers are equal, `SEQV` converting each into its bits and comparing those, and two equal rationals built apart are `SEQV` in the same way. The specification's list in `Specification/basic/objects.tex` ("Reference objects include arbitrary-precision numbers") is revised to name them among the value objects, in the revision form (P-96) with one Appendix I entry, in the rung that fixes what `SEQV` means (P-162). Why: the library's `value` declaration is the deliberate word, and where it is, the curator's rule brings the specification's example in line with the code. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4, point 11, which found the split.

# The carrier of `Any`: the design for the curator's decision

The tree is `main` at `16dfc29b7`. Its build is current: `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` and `default_repository/caches/implementation.stamp` both read `180a6844e44e…`. No source, library, test, specification or model file changed between the hard-set review's base `fc9b9293c` and this tree. Every Fortress run below used that build with a private caches folder, copied from the warm caches, or empty for the model's checks. The programs are scratch files and are not committed; each point quotes the lines that matter and the output. Three kinds of scratch code were put ahead of the build on the class path: a counter (section 5), and two prototypes, A and C, each a copy of one or two classes of the tree with a few lines changed (section 6). A prototype's library change was made in copies of `FortressBuiltin.fss` and `FortressLibrary.fss` in a scratch folder, which walk reads before the library because it searches the current folder first. Nothing in the tree changed. A Java path without a prefix is under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

## 1. The question, and a primer

**The question.** How do `Object`'s getters `ilkName` and `asString` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:38-41`) and `opr SEQV(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4650-4651`) leave walk's glue classes, so that both paths run them? And what does `SEQV` mean? P-162 left the three on glue "until a carrier of `Any` for both paths is designed", and said that the design also settles `SEQV`'s meaning [1].

**The words.**

1. *Walk* is Fortress's interpreter. The *compiled path* compiles a program to JVM bytecode and runs that. Each path has its own library today. At the *switch-over* the compiled path moves onto walk's library, the *one library*, and the compiler's own small library, the *prelude*, is deleted. The switch-over waits until every native binding of the one library has a binding that the compiled path runs [2].
2. A *native binding* is a library declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names the Java code that does the work [3].
3. A *glue class* is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` that takes walk's own run-time values. Only walk can run it. A compile refuses a glue string: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.' [4]
4. A *helper* is a public static Java method under `nativeHelpers/`. Both paths can call it. Walk calls it through its *loader*, `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java`, by reflection. The compiled path *rewrites* the body at the parse into a call of the helper, and the checker checks the declaration against the helper's Java signature [5].
5. P-58, a decision of the curator, says that every native binding names a helper and keeps the form `builtinPrimitive("…")`, and that walk loads the named helper. A *bare* binding is one whose body is exactly that call with a helper's name [6].
6. A *carrier* is the Java type in which walk's loader passes a value of a declared Fortress type to a helper: `ZZ32` in `int`, `RR64` in `double`, `FlatString` in `String`, and so on. Walk's loader reads a declared type by its name and refuses a binding with a declared type that no carrier names. No carrier names `Any` or `Object` [7].
7. A *transfer* is an identity helper that the compiled path puts around an argument or a result, so that the checker reads a Java `int` as `NN32` or `Char`. Transfers are not needed for these three [8].
8. A *representation* is the Java class of a run-time value. Walk's values are subclasses of `FValue` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/`): `FInt`, `FFloat`, `FString`, `FTuple`, `FOrdinaryObject` and others. The compiled path's values are classes that implement `fortress.AnyType.Any`: `FZZ32`, `FRR64` (`compiler/runtimeValues/`) and the classes that the code generator writes. Neither path's values are the other's [9].
9. `SEQV` is *object equivalence*, also written `===` and U+2263. The parser reads both spellings as one operator: under walk, where the library declares only `opr SEQV`, `three === three` and `3 === 3.0` both run, `12 ===: true true`; compiled, where the prelude declares only `opr ===`, `x SEQV y` runs, `8 SEQV spelling:  true` [10].
10. A *rung* is one task that one agent builds and lands with its tests. A *batch* is a set of rungs built at once [11].

**The example.**

11. One program, run on both paths [12]:

        object Pt(x: ZZ32, y: ZZ32) end
        ...
          p = Pt(1, 2); q = Pt(1, 2); x: ZZ32 = 3; y: ZZ32 = 3; r: RR64 = 3.0
          println(p.asString)
          println("SEQV: " (p SEQV p) " " (p SEQV q) " " (x SEQV y) " " (x SEQV r) " " ((x, y) SEQV (x, y)))

        walk:      Pt
                   SEQV: true false true true true
        compiled:  Pt
                   SEQV:  true   false   true   false   false

    Both paths print the object's type name, and both find a reference object equivalent only to itself. They differ on a `ZZ32` 3 beside an `RR64` 3.0, and on two equal tuples. (The compiled spaces around each value are row 76, the prelude's juxtaposition.)

**Why the three have no bare helper.**

12. The compiled path already has a helper for each: `stringOps.typeName` for `ilkName`, `stringOps.defaultAsString` for `asString`, and `equality.sEquiv` for `SEQV`, each over `fortress.AnyType.Any`. A program's own bindings of the three, at `Any`, compile and run: `1 typeName, defaultAsString:  Pt   Pt   ZZ32   3   Qt`, where `Qt` is the `self` of a program's trait. Under walk the same program stops at load: 'Native helper com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.typeName: no Java type carries the declared type of parameter x.' Walk's values are not `fortress.AnyType.Any`, and its loader has no carrier for `Any` [13].

## 2. The three today on each path

### 2.1 The declarations and walk's glue

1. **The declarations.** `trait Object extends Any` declares `getter ilkName(): String` on `ObjectPrims$ClassName` and `getter asString(): String` on `ObjectPrims$ToString`. Beside them, in Fortress, `asDebugString` is an article, `ilkName`, `": "` and `asString`; `asExprString` is `"no expression for "` and `asString`; the deprecated `toString` is `self.asString`. `opr SEQV(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean` is bound to `AnyPrim$SEquiv`, and its api line is `FortressLibrary.fsi:2645` [1].
2. **The glue.** `ToString` answers `o.toString()` and `ClassName` answers `o.type().toString()`. For a walk object, `FObject.toString()` is `getString()`, which is `type().toString()`, unless the value's class overrides `getString`. So both getters answer the type's name for every ordinary object. `AnyPrim.sequiv(x, y)` answers `true` if `x == y`, and otherwise `x.seqv(y)`: each value class of walk answers `SEQV` by its own method [2].
3. **Which values reach `Object`'s two getters.** Walk's classes that override `getString` are its number, `Boolean`, `Char` and string classes. Each of their library types declares its own `asString`: `Float`, `FloatLiteral`, `RR32`, `Int`, `Long`, `NN32`, `UnsignedLong`, `IntLiteral`, `BigNum`, `Boolean`, `Char` and `FlatString`. So only values whose type declares no `asString` reach `Object`'s, and for each of them `asString` and `ilkName` give one text. The counter of section 5, run on the program of section 2.2, met `ObjectPrims$ToString` only on `FOrdinaryObject` values: `Blank`, `Box[\ZZ32\]`, `Circ`, `Pt` and `VPlain` [3].

### 2.2 Walk's answers

4. **At work under walk**, with `object Pt(x: ZZ32, y: ZZ32)`, `object Blank`, `object Box[\T\](v: T)`, `value object VPlain(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32) end`, `value object VField(a, b)` with a body field, `object Circ(r) extends Shape`, `object Named(n)` with its own `asString`, and `inc(x: ZZ32): ZZ32` [4]:

        1 ilkName: Pt Blank Box[\ZZ32\] Box[\FlatString\] VPlain Circ Int FlatString Boolean Char FloatLiteral BigNum
        2 asString: Pt Blank Box[\ZZ32\] VPlain Circ Named x
        3 asString = ilkName: true true true
        4 asDebugString: a Pt: Pt; a Named: Named x; a Int: 3
        5 numbers: 3,3 true; ZZ32,ZZ64 true; ZZ32,RR64 true; ZZ32,NN32 false; ZZ,ZZ apart true; ZZ32,ZZ false; 0.0,-0.0 false; NaN,NaN true; 0.0 = -0.0 true
        6 tuples: true true true false true
        7 strings: true true false true CatString FlatString
        8 chars, booleans: true true false
        9 objects: true false true true false true false true
        10 functions: true true false
        11 default =: false true true

5. **What the lines show.**
    - Line 1: `ilkName` names walk's own class of a number, `Int`, `FloatLiteral`, `BigNum`, not `ZZ32`, `RR64` or `ZZ`; an inferred static argument is the run-time class, `Box[\FlatString\]` (row 364).
    - Line 5: a `ZZ32` 3 is equivalent to a `ZZ64` 3 and to an `RR64` 3.0, but not to an `NN32` 3 or a `ZZ` 3. Two `ZZ` 3s built apart are equivalent. Floats compare by their bits: `0.0` and `-0.0` are not equivalent, though `=` holds; a NaN is equivalent to itself.
    - Line 6: `(1,2)` and `(1,2)`, `(1,2)` and `(1,2.0)`, and `()` and `()` are equivalent; tuples of two equal `Pt`s are not.
    - Line 7: two flat strings of one text are equivalent; two equal strings longer than 32 characters are ropes, `CatString` objects, and are not.
    - Line 9: `p SEQV p` true, `p SEQV q` false, `Blank SEQV Blank` true; `VPlain(1,2) SEQV VPlain(1,3)` true and `Just(1) SEQV Just(2)` true, row 113's defect; `VField(1,2) SEQV VField(1,3)` false; two `Box[\ZZ32\](1)` false.
    - Line 10: a function value is equivalent to itself; two equal lambdas are not.
    - Line 11: `p = q` is `false` and `VPlain(1,2) = VPlain(1,3)` `true`, because the library's `=` at `Any` is `a SEQV b` [5].

### 2.3 The compiled path's answers

6. **The prelude.** `Object`'s `asString` is `jDefaultAsString(self)`, over `stringOps.defaultAsString`: the value's own Java `toString` if its class declares one, else its Fortress type name. `asDebugString` is `self.asString`; the team's article form, which reads `ilkName`, is commented out, and the prelude declares no `ilkName`. `SEQV` is the family `opr ===` under the comment "This is incomplete": at `Any` over `equality.sEquiv`, which answers `a == b`, and at `ZZ64`, `ZZ32`, `RR64`, `RR32` and `String` by `=`, at `Boolean` by `<->`. A commented `opr SEQV(a:Any, b:Any) = jSEQV(a,b)` names an alias that no import gives [6].
7. **At work compiled** [7]:

        1 asString:  Pt   Blank   Box[\ZZ32\]
        2 asDebugString:  Pt
        3 numbers: ZZ32,ZZ32  true ; ZZ32,ZZ64  false ; ZZ32,RR64  false ; 0.0,-0.0  true ; NaN,NaN  false

Mixed types and tuples fall to `Any`, where two boxes are compared as references. At line 7 the static types are `Any` and the dispatch method chooses by run-time type, so two `ZZ32` 3s still reach the `ZZ32` declaration.
8. **`ilkName` compiled.** `println(Pt(1, 2).ilkName)` is refused: 'Pt has no getter called ilkName', 'compile rc=255' [8].

### 2.4 What `SEQV` means: the specification, walk and the compiled path

10. **The specification's rule.** The trait `Any` declares `SEQV`. "This operator is automatically defined for all objects; it is a static error for the programmer to override it." Arguments of different dynamic types, "including the instantiations of all static parameters", are never equivalent. Value objects of one type are equivalent when their fields are, "in particular, two binary words are strictly equivalent if and only if they contain the same bit pattern". Two references are equivalent when they refer to one object. Two functions are equivalent only if they behave alike, and an implementation may answer `false` even then. The Working Draft has the same text [10].
11. **Which values are value objects.** A function object has an arrow type; a reference object has an object trait type not declared `value`; every other value is a value object, tuples and `()` among them. "booleans, numeric literals, IEEE floating-point numbers, and integers are value objects"; "Reference objects include arbitrary-precision numbers and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets". The chapter opens "Value objects and properties are not yet supported." The library declares `value object Int`, `Boolean`, `Char` and `BigNum`, and `object FlatString` without `value` [11].
12. **The three side by side.** "Spec" applies points 10 and 11; "walk" and "compiled" are the runs of points 4 and 7 [12]:

    | `VPlain(1,2)`, `VPlain(1,3)` | false, fields differ | true, row 113 | the `value` modifier has no effect |

Three principles settle a fork: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and the peers, which weigh only where the team's texts conflict or are silent. A fork is settled where the principles that speak to it point the same way. This section reads the first two and the specification; section 4 reads the peers [1].

### 3.1 Walk and its library as the team wrote them

1. **The first `SEQV`.** On 2008-03-04 Jan-Willem Maessen bound `opr SEQUIV(a:Any, b:Any)` to `AnyPrim$SEquiv`: "Preliminary (unsatisfactory) implementation of SEQUIV … Still to do: correct handling of value objects and closures." Its body already compared an integer with a float by value, `x.getFloat()==y.getFloat()` [2].
2. **The team's test.** Two days later he added `tests/sequivTest.fss`, "a shakedown test for SEQV (whose spelling has been corrected to match the spec); still don't check field matching for value types, or environment matching for closures." It asserts that a `ZZ32` 45 is equivalent to an `RR64` 45.0 and to a `ZZ64` 45: six of its lines assert numbers of different types equivalent. `ant testSystem` runs every program in `tests/`, so the test is gated today [3].
3. **Each value class answers `SEQV`.** On 2008-03-12 Maessen wrote: "SEQV now handles value objects correctly, traversing their fields when the types match. Re-factored seqv into a method of FValue in order to make sure that future primitive objects remember to implement it correctly." So walk's run time answers `SEQV` in each value class, and the glue only calls it [4].
4. **`Object`'s getters.** On 2008-07-29 Maessen added the type `Object`, whose "only method (concrete, built-in magic by default) is toString()". On 2008-08-27 the committer `black`, whom the authorship notes take, unconfirmed, for Andrew P. Black, "Added various printing functions and ilkName, for use in debugging." Both getters are walk's own rendering of a value's type [5].

### 3.2 The team's later word: the type group's compiled path, 2009 and 2010

5. **A helper over Java `Object`, 2009.** On 2009-06-09 Eric Allen wrote the first compiled helper, `equality.SEQV(Object a, Object b)`, `return a.equals(b)`, with "TODO Change this to call .SEQV methods, once they become available". Its prelude line was written commented out [6].
6. **`SEQV` is the language's own, 2009.** On 2009-06-30 Sukyoung Ryu made the checker refuse a `SEQV` declared in a trait or object, 'The object equivalence operator, SEQV, should not be overridden.', with the comment "TODO: check there is no top-level operator definition for SEQV when we have a better magic" [7].
7. **The prelude's family, 2010.** On 2010-05-05 David Chase "Added definition of === for popular types": the family of section 2.3, point 6, under "(* This is incomplete *)", and `equality.sEquiv`, `return a == b`, with "Eventually need to deal with tuples, value types, etc.". Two days later he moved its widest member from `Object` to `Any` [8].
8. **`asString` in the prelude, 2011 and 2012.** At the team's last commit `Object`'s `asString` was `jAsString(self)`, over `stringOps.asString`, `a.toString()`, the compiled run time's own Java text of a value, with the comments "this can't be right! DRC" and "I think this is better CHF". `ilkName` stays commented out inside `asDebugString`. The revival replaced `jAsString` by `defaultAsString` on 2026-09-23 (`6bec1b004`), for P-91 [9].

### 3.3 The specification

9. The rule of section 2.4, point 10: `SEQV` is "automatically defined for all objects", and overriding it is a static error. The sentence came with the 1.0 text, imported on 2009-11-06, and stands in the Working Draft [10].
10. The trait `Any` declares `toString(): String`, whose "general contract … is that it returns a string that 'textually represents' this object". The library's name for it is `asString`; its `toString` is `self.asString`, "deprecated". The specification names no `ilkName` [11].

### 3.4 Which way they point

11. **Where `SEQV` lives.** The specification defines it for every value and forbids a program to override it. Walk's design answers it in each value class (point 3). Allen's TODO wants the same on the compiled path, ".SEQV methods" (point 5). Ryu's TODO wants no top-level definition at all, "when we have a better magic" (point 6). The library as the team wrote it declares `SEQV` once, at `Any`, on a native. Chase's family is code that its author called incomplete, which serves the implementation only (P-26). So both principles point to one declaration at `Any`, answered by each path's run time in each value class. That settles where the operation lives. It rules out a family of overloads in the library, and does not choose how a binding reaches each run time's operation [12].
12. **What `SEQV` means.** The Working Draft (2011) and Chase's family (2010) agree that values of different types are not equivalent and that numbers of one type compare by value. Walk's code and test of 2008 say otherwise, and are earlier. By P-26 the later word wins: a `ZZ32` 3 and an `RR64` 3.0 are not equivalent. The specification states the bit pattern for floats and fields for value objects, tuples among them. Chase's `=` for floats and references for tuples are in the code that he called incomplete, and `equality.java` names tuples as still to do. So the rule stands there too. Two kinds stay split: strings and `ZZ` (section 2.4, point 13). The team's texts do not settle them [13].
13. **`asString` and `ilkName`.** The team's word gives both to the run time: walk's `type().toString()`, and on the compiled path a value's Java `toString`. P-91 fixed the text: an object with no `asString` of its own prints its bare type name, walk's spelling, on both paths. That is the text that `ilkName` gives (section 2.2, line 3). The team's texts do not say whether `asString` is a native or Fortress over `ilkName`. So the peers weigh there [14].

1. **Java.** Identity is a JVM instruction: `Objects.equals` begins `aload_0`, `aload_1`, `if_acmpeq`. `getClass()` and `hashCode()` are `native`. `Object.toString()` is bytecode over them: `getClass`, `Class.getName`, `"@"`, `hashCode`. Each option says how the three leave glue and what it does to `SEQV`'s meaning. Options (a) to (d) are the four ways that this review was asked to weigh; (e) cuts the number of natives, and combines with (a), (b) or (c).

### (a) A Java `Object` carrier in walk's loader, and one helper that reads both representations

1. **What it is.** Walk's loader carries `Any` and `Object` in a Java `Object` and passes walk's value itself. One helper per operation takes `Object` parameters and asks which representation it holds: a `fortress.AnyType.Any` takes the compiled operation, an `FValue` walk's. The three bindings name these helpers, bare [1].
2. **Measured, prototype A.** Walk's half is four lines in a copy of the loader: `javaFor` reads `Any` and `Object`; `typeName` reads `Any`, which the tree holds as an `AnyType` node, not a `NamedType`; `carried` admits `Object`; `unbox` passes the value. The helper class is 22 lines. A program bound to it ran under walk: `1 ilkName, asString: Pt Pt Box[\ZZ32\] Int`, `2 SEQV: p,p true; p,q false; 3,3 true; 3,3.0 true; tuples true`. [2]

The first compile stopped: 'Can't generate header for method sEquiv with jvm desc =Ljava/lang/Object; stripped = AnyType$Any'. With two lines in a copy of `FortressMethodAdapter.java` that pass an `Object` parameter unconverted, it compiled and ran: `1 ilkName, asString:  Pt   Pt   Box[\ZZ32\]   ZZ32`, `2 SEQV: p,p  true ; p,q  false ; 3,3  false ; 3,3.0  false ; tuples  false`. This corrects the hard-set review's reading that "no design reads both": one does, with that converter [3].
4. **Its limits.** The helper class can hold no method over `FValue`, a private one included: the wrapper generator reads every method of the class, and a compile stopped, 'No Fortress type (yet) for foreign Java type descriptor 'Lcom/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/FValue;''. F-321 says the same for the checker. So walk's reading sits inline in each public method, or in another class. No class under `nativeHelpers/` depends on walk's classes today, 0 of 26; this one would. <!-- The review for the curator's decision on whether Fortress strings are value objects or reference objects under strict equivalence, `SEQV`, that is, whether `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is true for two strings built apart, before the rung that fixes what `SEQV` means (P-162; `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, option (c)) joins climb batch 27; written 2026-11-06 by an Opus worker, reading only, with walk and compiled runs and two scratch library prototypes from the main tree's build at `a959ab2aa` in private caches folders. -->

# Strings under `SEQV`: value or reference, for the curator's decision

The tree is `main` at `a959ab2aa`. Its build is current: `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` and `default_repository/caches/implementation.stamp` both read `180a6844e44e…`. Every program below is a scratch file under `tmp/streqv/`, not committed. Each point quotes its output. A Java path without a prefix is under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

## 1. The question and a primer

**The question.** Is `"ab" SEQV "ab"` true for two strings built apart? If yes, strings are value objects under `SEQV`. If no, they are reference objects.

**The words.**

1. *`SEQV`* is strict equivalence, also called object equivalence. Its symbol is ≣, U+2263, "strictly equivalent to". `SEQV` and `===` are its ASCII spellings (`parser/Literal.rats:303`; `parser_util/precedence_resolver/Operators.java:2109`). Note: it is not ≡, U+2261. The parser reads `EQV` and `EQUIV` as ≡, a different operator (`Literal.rats:301-302`).
2. *Value object*: an object with no identity. Two of them built apart can be the same. *Reference object*: an object with an identity. Two of them built apart are always different.
3. *Walk* is the interpreter. The *compiled path* compiles to JVM bytecode. Each has its own library today. The compiled one is the *prelude*. At the *switch-over* the compiled path moves onto walk's library, and the prelude goes (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md`, "The phases").
4. A *flat string* is one Java string (`object FlatString`). A *rope* is a tree of strings (`object CatString`). A *substring* is a view into another string (`object SubString`).

**The specification's rule.** `Specification/basic/objects.tex:424-445`, "Object Equivalence":

> The trait Any declares the object equivalence operator ≣. This operator is automatically defined for all objects; it is a static error for the programmer to override it.

So `SEQV` is the one comparison that every value has. A program may not override it. The rule, in short:

- Different dynamic types, "including the instantiations of all static parameters": always false.
- Two value objects of one type: true "if and only if corresponding fields of the objects are themselves equivalent"; "two binary words are strictly equivalent if and only if they contain the same bit pattern" (so floats by their bits).
- Two references: true "if and only if the two object references refer to the identical reference object".
- Two functions: true only if they behave alike, and "the fortress implementation is free to return false".

**Which objects are value objects.** `objects.tex:22-31`: an object is "a reference object if it has an object trait type that is not declared with the `value` modifier", and a value object if it is a tuple, `()`, or declared `value`. The section "Value Objects" (`:347-422`) defines the modifier.

**The chapter's opening line.** `objects.tex:15`: "Value objects and properties are not yet supported."

**Why strings are the open kind.** The examples name booleans, numeric literals, floats and integers as value objects (`:39-43`). They name "arbitrary-precision numbers and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets" as reference objects (`:52-54`). They never name strings. Just before that list the text asks itself: "What about reference objects that have no mutable fields?" (`:51`). Strings are exactly that kind.

## 2. The library's declarations

| Declaration | File and line | `value`? |
|---|---|---|
| `trait String` | `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4341`, `.fsi:2447` | no |
| `object FlatString` | `Library/FlatString.fss:34`, `.fsi:16` | no |
| `object CatString(first, second)` | `Library/String.fss:75`, `.fsi:25` | no |
| `object SubString(baseString, range)` | `Library/String.fss:353`, `.fsi:34` | no |
| `value object EmptyString` | `Library/String.fss:282`, `.fsi:28` | yes |

So the library is split. Its empty string is a value object. Its other three are reference objects by the specification's definition.

**How a string's `=` is defined.**

1. `FlatString` declares `opr =(self, other: FlatString)` on the glue class `FlatString$Eq` (`FlatString.fss:70-71`). That class is Java's `self.equals(other)`, text equality (`interpreter/glue/prim/FlatString.java:131-136`). Its `<`, `>`, `CMP` use `cmp`, the helper `stringOps.compareTo` (`FlatString.fss:72-76`, `:85-86`).
2. `trait String` declares no `=` itself. It declares `CMP` character by character (`FortressLibrary.fss:4368-4369`). It inherits `=` from `StandardPartialOrder`: `opr =(self, other:T) = EqualTo = (self CMP other)` (`:232`). That is text equality for any two strings, of any shape.
3. There is no top-level `=` over `(String, String)` in walk's library (a grep for `opr =(` with `String` finds only `FlatString.fss:70` and `CaseInsensitiveString.fss:30`).
4. The fallback `opr =(a:Any, b:Any) = a SEQV b` (`FortressLibrary.fss:96`) and `Equality`'s `= ... self SEQV other` (`:101`) never see two strings: `StandardPartialOrder`'s `=` is more specific.

**Strings are immutable.** The string objects declare no `var` field (the `var`s in `String.fss` belong to `BalancingForest`, `:185-186`, `StringStats`, `:510-514`, and locals). The specification lists `String` with `Character` and the numerals among the "simple standard types for literals", and says "Values of these types are immutable" (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:572-581`).

## 3. What each runtime does today

**Walk's code.** `interpreter/evaluator/values/FString.java:35-38`:

```java
public boolean seqv(FValue v) {
    if (!(v instanceof FString)) return false;
    return (getString().equals(v.getString()));
}
```

That is text equality for two flat strings. `AnyPrim.sequiv` tests identity first, then calls `seqv` (`interpreter/glue/prim/AnyPrim.java:23-26`). Author: Jan-Willem Maessen (`jmaessen`), 2008-03-12, commit `cd41f90eb`, "SEQV now handles value objects correctly ... Re-factored seqv into a method of FValue". `git blame` stops at the cut root `5a68404fd`; `git show cd41f90eb -- '*FString.java'` adds these four lines. His first `SEQV`, 2008-03-04 (`d56a402b4`), already compared strings by text: `return (y instanceof FString) && x.getString().equals(y.getString());`.

A rope or a substring is not an `FString`. It is a library object, an `FOrdinaryObject`. Its `seqv` answers false unless its type is declared `value` (`FOrdinaryObject.java:46-57`). So walk compares a rope by identity.

**The prelude's code.** `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:62-71`, under "(* This is incomplete *)":

```
opr ===(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = jSEQUIV(a,b)
...
opr ===(a:String, b:String):Boolean = a=b
```

Author: David Chase (`dr2chase`), 2010-05-05, commit `64e5f04db`, "Added definition of === for popular types" (`git log -S'opr ===(a:String, b:String)'`, its oldest entry). The line stands unchanged at the team's last commit (`git show a874948ac:Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`, line 68). Beside it, `jSEQUIV` is `equality.sEquiv`, which compares references: `return a == b;`, with "Eventually need to deal with tuples, value types, etc." (`nativeHelpers/equality.java:14-19`). The prelude's own `trait String` has a placeholder `=` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:395`); its `JavaString` compares by `jCompareTo` (`:428`).

**Walk's answers.** `tmp/streqv/StrEqvWalk.fss`, run as `bin/fortress walk StrEqvWalk.fss` with the setup lines. `rope1` is `"abcdefghij" || "klmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMN"`, past `maxLeafSize`, 32 (`String.fss:576`), so `FlatString`'s `||` builds a `CatString` (`FlatString.fss:121-129`). `rope2` is the same text split 30 and 10. `sub1` is `rope1[5#10]`, which crosses the halves, so `CatString.uncheckedSubstring` builds a `SubString` (`String.fss:148-161`).

```
1 flat, flat built apart: true =: true same: true
3 flat, rope: false =: true
4 rope, rope, other shape: false =: true
5 rope, rope, same shape built apart: false =: true same: true
7 sub, sub built apart: false =: true
8 sub, flat: false =: true
9 EmptyString, EmptyString: true; EmptyString, "": false =: true
10 tuples: true ropes in tuples: false
12 as Any: false numbers: true pair: true
rc=0
```

Line 2 printed the shapes: `J40/0:` for the flat string, `BC40/1:` with two leaves for each rope; line 6 printed `S10= [5:14]` for the substring. 1. `ProjectFortress/tests/sequivTest.fss` (Maessen, 2008-03-06, `21946c933`) has no line on strings. Its values are numbers, an array, functions, tuples, booleans and `Maybe`s (`:29-114`). It is gated.
